title: University of El Segundo — Coffee business studies, first edition
research_scope: Six official indicators covering El Segundo, the Los Angeles metropolitan area, California, U.S. retail coffee prices, and the global green-coffee market. This is a bounded source-backed teaching edition, not a local business census or shop revenue database.
editorial_rules: Show the report period and observation date separately next to every statistic.
Mark USDA production and consumption figures as forecasts. Do not present them as realized 2026/27 outcomes.
Use merchant-owned published menus and product pages for assortment examples; availability is dated and partial.
Company revenue, sales, inventory counts, margins, footfall, payroll and customer retention are unknown unless a public source specifically establishes them.
Every numerical business model below is invented for teaching and is unrelated to any named shop.
IndustryNext and University of El Segundo are editorial destinations, not a claim of accreditation, affiliation with a public university, or merchant endorsement.

The café calculator uses the agreed $7 ticket, 180 daily transactions, 26 operating days, 30% variable costs and $19,000 fixed budget including labor and occupancy. Keep the calculator and displayed worked example synchronized.

facts.title: U.S. retail coffee prices
facts.summary: The national coffee CPI-U category increased 6.1% over twelve months. Its August month-to-month change was −0.9% before seasonal adjustment.
facts.interpretation: A household retail-price signal for coffee purchased for home use; useful for discussing consumer substitution and price transmission.
facts.limitations: It is not a café menu-price index, wholesale bean quote, dollar price per pound, local demand measure or shop margin.
facts.claim: The national coffee CPI-U category increased 6.1% over twelve months. Its August month-to-month change was −0.9% before seasonal adjustment.
facts.caveat: It is not a café menu-price index, wholesale bean quote, dollar price per pound, local demand measure or shop margin.

facts.title: Los Angeles food service price backdrop
facts.geography: Los Angeles–Long Beach–Anaheim; Los Angeles and Orange counties
facts.summary: The area's food-away-from-home CPI-U increased 2.4% over twelve months and was unchanged from July to August.
facts.interpretation: A broad restaurant-price comparison for classroom discussion of a café's pricing choices.
facts.limitations: The metro index is broader than coffee, is not seasonally adjusted, and has a smaller sample than the national CPI. It does not measure an El Segundo café or compare price levels between cities.

facts.title: California general wage floor
facts.summary: California's general minimum wage is $16.90 per hour for employers outside a higher industry or local wage requirement.
facts.interpretation: An input to labor-cost scenario design, before payroll taxes, benefits, coverage, training and scheduling.
facts.limitations: Some localities and industries have higher requirements. Do not apply this general floor to every café or chain; verify the workplace and applicable rules. The calculator’s $19,000 fixed budget is an invented teaching assumption, not a statutory wage or reported shop payroll.
facts.claim: California's general minimum wage is $16.90 per hour for employers outside a higher industry or local wage requirement.
facts.caveat: Some localities and industries have higher requirements. Do not apply this general floor to every café or chain; verify the workplace and applicable rules. The calculator’s $19,000 fixed budget is an invented teaching assumption, not a statutory wage or reported shop payroll.

facts.title: El Segundo resident context
facts.summary: Census estimates 16,379 city residents on July 1, 2025. The 2020–2024 median household income is $150,737 in 2024 dollars.
facts.interpretation: Resident-market context for a catchment exercise.
facts.limitations: City residents are not the population of the 25-mile atlas. Household income is not individual purchasing power; neither figure counts café customers, commuters, airport visitors or daytime workers. Five-year income estimates are historical averages.
facts.claim: Census estimates 16,379 city residents on July 1, 2025. The 2020–2024 median household income is $150,737 in 2024 dollars.
facts.caveat: City residents are not the population of the 25-mile atlas. Household income is not individual purchasing power; neither figure counts café customers, commuters, airport visitors or daytime workers. Five-year income estimates are historical averages.

facts.title: Global supply outlook
facts.summary: USDA forecasts 2026/27 world coffee production at 189.7 million bags and consumption at 179.7 million bags; each bag is 60 kilograms.
facts.interpretation: Use the forecast to discuss procurement planning and the uncertainty between crop expectations and delivered costs.
facts.limitations: Forecasts can change. Marketing-year calendars vary by country. Production minus consumption is not a shop profit, delivered inventory forecast or complete stocks/trade accounting. Do not splice these figures with ICO coffee-year balances without explaining their different periods and methods.

facts.title: Global green-coffee price signal
facts.summary: ICO's composite green-coffee indicator averaged 287.29 US cents per pound in August, compared with 287.26 in July.
facts.interpretation: A benchmark for discussing exposure to global bean-price movements.
facts.limitations: The composite is not the invoice price of a specialty lot or roasted bag. Differentials, quality, contracts, currency, freight, yield loss and timing affect a roaster's actual cost.

outlook.label: Source-based classroom interpretation, not a sales forecast
outlook.local: Start with distinct resident, workplace, visitor and neighborhood catchments. Census city figures help frame the resident segment; the 25-mile radius needs its own geography and does not establish trade areas.
outlook.regional: A café's menu-price decision can be compared with metro food service inflation, while its own mix and customer response remain unknown.
outlook.state: Use the applicable workplace wage requirements when designing the labor budget. The calculator includes all scheduled labor inside its fixed-cost assumption; a wage floor alone cannot establish that budget.
outlook.national: Retail coffee inflation and café demand are different measures. The national coffee category can inform a discussion of home-brew substitution without proving that a named café gained or lost customers.
outlook.global: Supply forecasts and a nearly unchanged monthly green-coffee indicator can coexist with higher annual retail prices. Timing and the path from green beans to a finished product matter.
outlook.refresh_guidance: This edition was observed October 3, 2026. Recheck BLS after the scheduled October 14 CPI release, USDA after its scheduled December 16 circular, and ICO when the next report appears; these are source release notes, not promises that the atlas is live.

business_models.name: Neighborhood café
business_models.revenue_mechanism: Immediate sale of a prepared drink; food and retail bags can change the basket.
business_models.operating_constraint: Peak-hour queue and service capacity, plus enough traffic outside the peak to cover the schedule.
business_models.lesson: Measure contribution per order and contribution per scheduled labor hour together. A busy queue does not prove a profitable full day.
evidence_to_collect: Timed public observation of service flow without personal data
Voluntary merchant-provided aggregate data only if separately authorized
business_models.case_prompt: An independent café faces a bean-cost increase. Compare a menu adjustment, product mix change, and staffing schedule using the same demand scenarios.

business_models.name: Roastery with direct retail
business_models.revenue_mechanism: Transform purchased green coffee into branded roasted beans sold directly.
cost_drivers: Quality control, equipment and working capital
business_models.lesson: Calculate yield before margin. A lower green-bean quote does not imply the same reduction in cost per sellable roasted pound.
evidence_to_collect: Published roast assortment and bag sizes
business_models.case_prompt: A roaster can add another origin or increase an existing batch. Compare inventory complexity, freshness risk and capacity use.

business_models.name: Roastery wholesale channel
business_models.revenue_mechanism: Repeat bulk orders from cafés, offices or hospitality accounts.
business_models.operating_constraint: Reliable production and delivery plus receivables.
business_models.lesson: Compare contribution after delivery and service with cash conversion. Larger volume can require more cash before payment arrives.
evidence_to_collect: Published minimums or service terms where available
Do not infer customer identities or contract prices
business_models.case_prompt: A wholesale account offers more volume at a lower price. Test the order after route cost, capacity and payment terms.

business_models.name: Direct coffee subscription
business_models.revenue_mechanism: Recurring shipments with a chosen cadence and published terms.
cost_drivers: Customer acquisition, cancellations and skipped cycles
business_models.lesson: Separate repeat contribution from acquisition payback. Count actual fulfilled cycles, including skips and refunds, before estimating lifetime value.
evidence_to_collect: No invented churn or subscriber counts
business_models.case_prompt: Compare a shipping-included subscription with local pickup. Model postage and replacement acquisition separately.

unit_economics.label: Illustrative classroom assumptions — not actual company sales or costs
common_notes: Exercises are independent; their purchase and sale prices are not transfer prices between these businesses.
Prices exclude sales taxes and tips. Every cost and volume below is an editable teaching assumption.
Contribution means sales price minus the listed variable costs. It is not net profit.
Final business viability also requires fixed costs, financing, equipment, owner compensation, taxes and a realistic capacity plan.
Round display values to cents; keep unrounded intermediate values for calculations.

cafe.unit: One transaction with a mixed beverage/food average ticket
cafe.label: Independent illustrative classroom scenario; not a named shop
cafe.formula: Monthly orders = daily transactions × operating days. Revenue = ticket × orders. Contribution = revenue × (1 − variable-cost fraction). Monthly result = contribution − fixed costs. Whole-order daily break-even = ceiling(fixed costs / (ticket × (1 − variable-cost fraction) × days)).
cafe.exclusions: Equipment purchase or depreciation, financing, income taxes, owner compensation if not budgeted in the fixed labor amount, and any unlisted cost. All scheduled labor and occupancy must be inside the stated fixed budget; do not add an extra payroll allocation.
cafe.capacity_note: Fixed cost is an assumed schedule and occupancy budget. Increased volume may require a new staffing tier or equipment; recalculate fixed costs when capacity changes. A percentage variable cost is a simplification, especially when price changes while physical inputs stay similar.

sensitivity.scenario: Fixed labor and occupancy budget rises 15%

roastery_direct.unit: One 12-ounce (0.75-pound) roasted bag; buyer-paid outbound shipping is treated as neutral
roastery_direct.formula: Green cost = roasted pounds / roast yield × green cost per pound. Listed variable cost = green cost + processing + packaging + payment.
roastery_direct.exclusions: Acquisition, fixed plant and equipment, unsold bags, customer-service overhead and any shipping subsidy. Processing allocation assumes a usable batch size; low utilization changes cost.

wholesale.formula: Contribution = price − (roasted pounds / yield × green cost + processing + bulk packaging + delivery + payment allowance).
wholesale.exclusions: Fixed plant, sales labor, account support, bad debt beyond the allowance and financing. Payment terms and delivery density must be modeled separately.

subscription.unit: One shipping-included order with two 12-ounce bags
subscription.formula: Shipment contribution = price − green cost − processing − packaging − postage − handling − payment. For a constant active subscriber base, replacement-acquisition allocation per active cycle = assumed lost-member rate × acquisition cost.
subscription.exclusions: Platform and fixed labor, discounts, skips, refund losses, failed payments and changes in shipping zones. The replacement rates and acquisition cost are invented assumptions, not observed churn or a lifetime-value estimate.

teaching_sessions.title: From an atlas pin to a business question
teaching_sessions.activity: Select a published café and a roaster from the atlas. Record only source-supported menu, bag-size, sourcing and channel claims; write unknown where the source is silent.
questions: What customer use case does the public assortment suggest?
How does a 25-mile geometric radius differ from a realistic café catchment?
Which additional evidence would be needed before claiming demand or profitability?

teaching_sessions.title: The morning queue
teaching_sessions.activity: Use the café model and compare bean-cost, wage, price and demand sensitivities. Keep the schedule fixed first, then test an added peak shift.
questions: Which assumption changes the result most in this exercise?
When might faster service raise orders without requiring more paid hours?
What evidence would show that a price increase improved total contribution rather than only contribution per order?

teaching_sessions.title: One batch, many channels
teaching_sessions.activity: Compare direct bags, wholesale pounds and two-bag subscriptions after converting all outputs to roasted weight. Preserve each channel's shipping, delivery and acquisition assumptions.
questions: Does the largest unit margin also have the lowest capital need?
How does yield loss change contribution across channels?
What happens when a wholesale customer pays later than the roaster pays suppliers?

teaching_sessions.title: Compare coffee and regulated retail
teaching_sessions.activity: Pair a coffee case with the separately verified dispensary case. Compare catchment, product-source freshness, payment, staffing, channel constraints and inventory risk using each case's own sources.
questions: Which metrics can be compared directly, and which require different definitions?
What makes an assortment snapshot different from live stock?
How would evidence quality change the decision even if the spreadsheet result stayed the same?

methodology.collection: Read official BLS, Census, California DIR, USDA FAS and ICO pages or reports directly. Search results alone were not treated as evidence. Merchant-specific cases must be grounded in the separate café/roaster source research.
methodology.date_handling: Observation date is October 3, 2026. Release dates, effective dates and statistical periods are independent fields. Unknown publication days remain null.
methodology.geography: Resident figures describe city limits; LA CPI describes a two-county metro area; state wage rules depend on workplace jurisdiction; national/global indicators do not resolve individual shops.
methodology.model_handling: All business-model numbers are hypothetical. Models deliberately omit actual merchant revenues and private financial data.
limitations: This is not an exhaustive census of cafés, roasters or market conditions.
No shop's stock, sales, revenue, employment or customer retention has been inferred.
Public assortment and opening-hour pages can become stale and require merchant rechecking.
Data from different agencies have different definitions and periods; forecasts cannot be compared as realized sales.
A sensitivity exercise illustrates a mechanism and cannot forecast a specific shop's outcome.
methodology.attribution: Use direct source links adjacent to each statistic. Paraphrase factual statements; no third-party artwork is included in this research file.
